sections.label: National and Presidential symbols
sections.summary: The Bill declares and regulates Singapore's national and Presidential symbols, noting three national symbols unveiled over 60 years ago.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
sentences.text: It will declare the national symbols and Presidential symbols of Singapore and regulate the use of these symbols.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
sentences.text: More than 60 years ago, our three national symbols were unveiled on the steps of City Hall at the inauguration of our first Malayan-born Yang di-Pertuan Negara (Head of State) Encik Yusof Ishak.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Low Yen Ling) (for the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth)
sentences.text: They were the state crest, the national flag and the national anthem.

sections.label: SAFNA Act and later symbols
sections.summary: The SAFNA Act 1959 governs the state crest, flag and anthem, while three more national symbols were introduced between 1966 and 1986.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: The Singapore Arms and Flag and National Anthem Act 1959, also known as the SAFNA Act, was enacted to govern the use of the state crest, the national flag and the national anthem.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: Between 1966 and 1986, we introduced three more national symbols outside the SAFNA Act: the national pledge, the national flower and the lion head symbol.

sections.label: Symbols given statutory protection
sections.summary: The Bill extends statutory recognition and protection to the national pledge, national flower, lion head symbol and public seal.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: The Bill will extend statutory recognition and protection to these familiar symbols which were not covered by SAFNA and they are the national pledge, the national flower, the lion head symbol and the public seal.

sections.label: Presidential symbols recognised
sections.summary: The Bill grants statutory recognition and protection to the Presidential standard, Presidential crest and Presidential seal as Presidential symbols.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: The Bill will also grant statutory recognition and protection to the Presidential standard, the Presidential crest and the Presidential seal as Presidential symbols.

sections.label: Updated SAFNA Act penalties
sections.summary: The Bill updates SAFNA Act offence penalties from a maximum $1,000 fine to a maximum $30,000 fine, six months' imprisonment, or both.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: The current penalty for offences under the SAFNA Act is a fine of up to $1,000 – a maximum fine of $1,000.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: Taking into account the maximum penalties that are set for similar offences, we will update the penalties for such offences to a maximum fine of $30,000 or a maximum imprisonment term of six months or both.

sections.label: Amendments to related legislation
sections.summary: The Bill amends the Evidence Act 1893 on the public and Presidential seals and renames the National Emblems (Control of Display) Act 1949.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: The Bill will also make the following amendments to related legislation – section 59(1)(f) of the Evidence Act 1893 will be amended to require the Courts to recognise the public seal and the Presidential seal.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: The National Emblems (Control of Display) Act 1949 will be renamed the "Foreign National Emblems (Control of Display) Act 1949" to make clear that its role is in regulating foreign national emblems.

sections.label: Wider use of national symbols
sections.summary: The speaker gives three suggestions and notes MCCY loosened approval requirements for wider use of national symbols after citizen feedback.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I have three suggestions and clarifications on the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: I am glad that MCCY listened to feedback from the citizens' workgroup and is allowing a wider use of our national symbols by loosening approval requirements.

sections.label: Accessible pre-approval process
sections.summary: The speaker asks how the Ministry will keep the pre-approval process accessible, low-cost and simple for well-intentioned individuals using national symbols.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Minister share how the Ministry will ensure that the pre-approval process is accessible, low-cost and simple to navigate for well-intentioned individuals who wish to use the national symbols?

sections.label: Punishments for misusing symbols
sections.summary: The speaker asks whether the Minister will consider enhanced punishments for those who misuse national symbols to mislead others.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Will the Minister consider creating enhanced punishments for those who misuse the national symbols to mislead others?

sections.label: President's power to amend symbols
sections.summary: The speaker asks when such an amendment is anticipated and on whose advice the President acts, noting the Bill gives statutory recognition to national symbols.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Can the Minister clarify in what circumstances is it anticipated that such an amendment may be made?

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: When the President exercises her or his powers to amend the symbols, on what basis and on which entity's or individual's advice will the President be acting?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It provides formal statutory recognition to our national symbols and seeks to clarify and broaden the use of the national symbols by Singaporeans to express national pride and solidarity.

sections.label: Educating on national anthem meaning
sections.summary: The speaker cites Pak Zubir Said's view of the anthem as a prayer and calls for more education on its meaning, noting many citizens do not know the words.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: For example, it is said that Pak Zubir Said, when he composed the national anthem, thought of it as a kind of prayer to be uttered when Singapore attained Independence.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And here, I would like to call for more efforts to be made to educate our people on the meaning of the national anthem.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It is sad that many citizens do not know the words or even what the words mean, simply referring to our anthem as "mari-kita." Sir, our pledge calls on all of us to be one people, regardless of race, language or religion.

sections.label: Galvanising respect for national symbols
sections.summary: The speaker argues that all who value democratic society should work towards galvanising respect for national symbols among fellow Singaporeans of all views.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Rather, I would like to argue today that all of us who value our democratic society, including all of us in this House, should work towards galvanising respect for our national symbols among our fellow Singaporeans, of all views and all shades of political opinion.

sections.label: Light touch enforcement hope
sections.summary: The speaker hopes authorities enforce the law lightly, showing compassion and considering individual circumstances like ignorance, mental illness or momentary emotions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: At this point, I would like to express the hope that the authorities take a light touch in enforcing the provisions of this law, show compassion and take cognisance of the individual circumstances associated with each offence, for example, where ignorance, mental illness or momentary emotions come into play.

sections.label: Support for National Symbols Bill
sections.summary: The Member states in Malay that they support the National Symbols Bill in making meaningful and necessary changes.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: (In Malay):   Madam, I support the National Symbols Bill in making meaningful and necessary changes.

sections.label: National symbols and political unity
sections.summary: The speaker says national symbols represent independence and sovereignty, and hopes citizens of all political leanings respect them through inspiration, not only law enforcement.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Because they symbolise our hard-fought Independence and our national sovereignty.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It is important because it is equivalent to our national freedom – our freedom to choose our own destiny as a people, through the institutions of our democratic society, the democratic society that we all pledged to build.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Today, I want to talk about how we should be one people, regardless of political views or affiliation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I can confidently say that from many conversations with Singaporeans, that displaying the flag is not associated with any political leanings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: And I have met many Singaporeans who are true patriots, who belong to different political parties.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It is my hope that all of us who have faith in this democratic society would serve as advocates and role models as citizens who believe that our national symbols should be respected by everyone, regardless of their political leanings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This can be achieved by inspiring our citizens about what Singapore is and what it can be, not through law enforcement, even though this, inevitably, has a role.

sections.label: Nurturing pledge ideals hope
sections.summary: The speaker says that despite robust debate over the pledge's ideals in policies, Singaporeans should nurture this hope in their hearts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: While we may disagree and debate robustly over what the ideals of our pledge concretely mean in day-to-day policies, we should strive to nurture this hope in our hearts and the hearts of fellow Singaporeans.

sections.label: Lion head symbol advertisements
sections.summary: The speaker notes past instances where the lion head symbol was used to promote products and services unrelated to the Government.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: One problematic area is that of commercial advertisements.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: There were instances in the past where the lion head symbol was used to promote products and services which had no relation with the Government.

sections.label: Guidelines for symbol and flag use
sections.summary: The speaker asks about users circumventing rules by using part of the symbol or different colours, and calls for more comprehensive guidelines for the flag's image.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Under the current circumstances, what if the users were to use part of the symbol or, for example, to use the symbol in different colours as they try to circumvent the rules?

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: We also need more comprehensive guidelines for the use of the flag's image without requiring official approval on attire, decoration and products.

sections.label: SAFNA Act prosecutions
sections.summary: Asks how many cases were prosecuted under the Singapore Arms and Flag and National Anthem Act and Rules for such offences in the past.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: How many cases were prosecuted under the Singapore Arms and Flag and National Anthem (SAFNA) Act and Rules for such offences in the past?

sections.label: National Emblems Act amendment
sections.summary: Asks how the National Emblems (Control of Display) Act 1949 will be amended.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: How will the National Emblems (Control of Display) Act 1949 be amended?

sections.label: Support for National Symbols Bill
sections.summary: States national symbols define and unify Singaporeans and expresses support for the Bill promoting appropriate use while allowing wider use.

sentences.speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
sentences.text: It allows us to demonstrate our patriotism and express pride in our unique multicultural and multi-religious society.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: These representations of our nationhood were developed because these visible, identifiable symbols are necessary in defining and unifying Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: As a multicultural and diverse nation, our national symbols have been instrumental in creating and cementing our identity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Therefore, I stand in support of the Bill, which seeks to promote appropriate use of national symbols while allowing for their wider use by Singaporeans to express national pride and solidarity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: This will give Singaporeans the clarity and flexibility in their use whilst preserving the honour and respect that our national symbols deserve.

sections.label: Additional protected national symbols
sections.summary: States the proposed National Symbols Bill accords protection to seven additional national symbols alongside the three originally protected under SAFNA.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Under the proposed National Symbols Bill, seven additional national symbols like the Presidential standard, Presidential coat of arms, Presidential seal, national pledge, public seal, lion head symbol and national flower will be accorded protection status alongside the three national symbols that are originally protected under SAFNA.

sections.label: National Day period extensions
sections.summary: States the National Day period was extended in 2007 and the rule amended in 2020 to allow flag display from April to June 2020.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: In 2007, the National Day period was extended from 1 July to 30 September, and, in 2020, the rule was amended to allow the flag to be displayed from April to June 2020 as a mark of solidarity during the COVID-19 crisis.

sections.label: Guidance on symbol offences
sections.summary: Says clear cases like willful flag defacing must be dealt with, but asks Government for guidance on respectful use and offences under the new law.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: On the issue of clarity, the disrespecting of national symbols in some cases, such as the willful and intentional defacing of the flag, for example, is quite clear and such cases must be dealt with accordingly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: However, as more symbols get designated as national symbols and come under the proposed new laws, it would be good if the Government could provide some guidance as to how the symbols should be used respectfully and just what constitutes an offence regarding the treatment of a national symbol under the new law.

sections.label: Lion head symbol usage
sections.summary: Asks whether using the lion head symbol would be allowed under the National Symbols Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Would such usage of the lion head symbol be allowed under the National Symbols Bill?

sections.label: National symbols guidance and awareness
sections.summary: Calls for clear government guidance and says freer everyday contact and public education can raise awareness of national symbols.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Again, I understand that one cannot have detailed prescriptions for everything, but it would be good if the Government could provide some clear guidance in this area.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: Many Singaporeans, and even foreigners, have come to associate the national symbols as synonymous with Singapore and the Singapore brand and what Singapore stands for.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: The national symbols are also cultural symbols, each capturing a unique portion of Singapore's history and the aspirations of our country and people.

sentences.speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: One of the approaches to increasing Singaporeans' awareness of the symbols is to allow them to come into contact with these symbols more freely and more spontaneously in their everyday lives and to conduct more public education on what the symbols mean.

sections.label: Clause 13 minor updates
sections.summary: Clause 13 of the Bill will likely be used only for minor and technical updates, such as enhancing digital file quality of official symbol images.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: Clause 13 of the Bill will likely only be used to make minor and technical updates when needed, for example, the enhancement of the digital file quality of the official images of the symbols.

sections.label: Amending symbols and adding new ones
sections.summary: Significant symbol changes will consider public views and consult Parliament, and Parliament must amend the Bill to add a new national symbol.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: In the event that any significant amendment to a symbol is being considered in accordance with the wishes of the people of Singapore, we will take the public's views into consideration and, if significant changes are needed, Parliament will be consulted.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: Mr Yip Hon Weng raised a related point, namely, whether the legislation would cover the addition and inclusion of newer symbols.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: I wish to clarify that Parliament will need to amend the Bill to add a new national symbol.

sections.label: Flag hanging and calibrated liberalisation
sections.summary: Respondents called flag-hanging during the National Day period a patriotic ritual, so a calibrated approach lowers barriers to common uses with safeguards.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: Some of the respondents and participants also highlighted that hanging the flag, when the National Day period – July, August, September – comes around every year, is a form of national ritual that affirms our patriotism and love for Singapore, not unlike the daily pledge-taking or singing of the national anthem in schools.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: We have, therefore, taken a calibrated approach towards liberalising the use of the national symbols by trying to lower the barriers to the most common uses, whilst putting in checks and balances, safeguards to protect the dignity and stature of our national symbols.

sections.label: Simplified guidelines for flag attire
sections.summary: The Bill plans simplified guidelines for respectful, non-commercial use of the flag image on attire, including sporting attire, without prior approval.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: Under the Bill, we plan to further streamline this process by having a simplified set of guidelines in place to facilitate the respectful and non-commercial use of the image of the flag on attire, including sporting attire, where users are not required to obtain any prior approval.

sections.label: Guidelines, stop orders, national symbols
sections.summary: Guidelines will address commercial use of anthem and pledge, and the Bill provides stop orders against disrespectful use of national symbols.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: For both the anthem and the pledge, the guidelines would also address questions on potential commercial uses of these symbols.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: We also intend to make provisions under the Bill for a stop order to be issued against disrespectful use of the national symbols.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: Failure to comply with a stop order would constitute an offence.

sections.label: Updated guidelines publication date
sections.summary: The updated guidelines will be published once the regulations under the Bill are enacted in 2023.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: The updated guidelines will be published once the regulations under the Bill are enacted in 2023.

sections.label: Higher penalties for egregious offences
sections.summary: Egregious offences like flag desecration or using state crest to misrepresent Government would attract higher penalties.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: In response to Mr Louis Ng's question whether the Government would consider creating an enhanced punishment for those who misuse the national symbols to mislead others, I would like to state that egregious offences like the desecration or deliberate burning of the flag, as well as the intentional use of the state crest, flag or Presidential symbols to misrepresent the Government or deceive the public, would attract higher penalties.

sections.label: Offences and penalties still deliberated
sections.summary: The precise offences and maximum penalties are still being deliberated and will be calibrated to be proportionate.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: The precise offences and maximum penalties for these offences are still being deliberated and will be carefully calibrated to ensure that they are proportionate.

sections.label: SAFNA Act investigations, no prosecutions
sections.summary: There have been Police investigations but no prosecutions or composition of offences under the SAFNA Act and Rules.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: To our knowledge, there have been Police investigations, but not prosecutions or composition of offences under the SAFNA Act and Rules.

sections.label: Renaming Act, public education focus
sections.summary: The Act will be renamed the Foreign National Emblems (Control of Display) Act 1949, and focus will be on public education.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: Under the Bill, that Act will be renamed the Foreign National Emblems (Control of Display) Act 1949 to make the distinction that it deals with foreign national emblems.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: More often than not, it is likely due to genuine mistakes.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: We have also received feedback through the Citizens' Workgroup and in-depth consultations with stakeholders that public education would be key to the success of this Bill – public education and raising public awareness.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: As such, while the proposed legislative changes, such as the stop order, aim to address concerns on possible misuse of the symbols, I want to assure Members that we will focus on public education to ensure that members of the public are aware of the guidelines and do not inadvertently use the flag or other symbols disrespectfully.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: We will, likewise, increase public awareness of how to suitably display national symbols like the flag, at relevant junctures, such as the National Day period.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: The National Symbols belong to all Singaporeans because they represent the values and ideals that we hold dear.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: We hope that the Bill will foster greater pride and the use of the national symbols among Singaporeans.
